transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-03-15 10:00 PT | Duration: 45 min | Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Chen (Lakeside CTO), Aisha Thompson (Product), Tom Rivera (Eng Mgr)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan Blake, AE at Redwood. With me is Priya Nair, our solutions engineer. How are you all doing?
[00:05] Mark: Good, thanks. Excited to see the demo. We're exploring a chat assistant and some summarize/rewrite text features for our shopping app.
[00:12] Jordan: Great. Quick agenda — we'll run through Hosted API basics for chat and text generation: streaming, common params like temperature and max_tokens, stop sequences, plus how we handle retries and idempotency. We'll also touch on SDK examples and cost/latency tradeoffs.
[00:25] Aisha: Sounds good. Our main constraints are p95 latency under 300ms for single-turn product suggestions and predictable cost.
[00:33] Priya: Cool. I'll share my screen and start with a short request example. Note: transcript may garble some code snippets.
[00:40] [screen share starts]
[00:45] Priya: This is our simple chat flow — short prompt with user context. We call the /v1/chat/completions endpoint. Key fields: messages, model, temperature, max_tokens, top_p, and stop. For streaming we open a server-sent events stream and get token deltas as they arrive.
[01:05] Tom: How does streaming affect latency and costs? If we stream, do we pay per token as it's generated?
[01:12] Priya: Yes, cost is per token generated regardless of streaming. Streaming helps user-perceived latency because you can show partial output sooner. It also allows progressive rendering and early stopping client-side. There is some added complexity in client code for handling events and reconnect logic.
[01:28] Mark: And in terms of reliability — what if the stream disconnects mid-response?
[01:33] Priya: Good question. We recommend idempotency keys for create calls and a retry strategy. For streaming specifically, if the connection drops you can either: 1) re-request with the same idempotency key and the server can resume or return the completed response depending on model and work done; or 2) fall back to a non-streaming call. Implementation details vary a bit by model and backend. Our SDKs include helpers for reconnect and resume where supported.
[01:56] Jordan: To add, we surface request-level metrics in the Console so you can see streaming success rates and reconnects.
[02:04] Aisha: You mentioned idempotency keys — do we need them for every call?
[02:09] Priya: We recommend for any request that mutates state or for long-running requests. For simple stateless chat generation it's optional but helpful for retries. Also, include a client-generated request_id header to map logs.
[02:25] Jordan: Let's demo parameter effects. I'll change temperature from 0.2 to 0.8 so you can see variance in creativity.
[02:33] Priya: Lower temperature gives more deterministic answers; higher yields more diverse outputs. Also show max_tokens — you can restrict length. Stop sequences are useful for structured outputs so the model doesn't keep going.
[02:50] Tom: How do stop sequences interact with streaming? If the model emits stop mid-token, do we get a clean cutoff?
[02:58] Priya: Streaming sends token deltas, so you'll see until the stop sequence is emitted as tokens. There are edge cases for tokenization boundaries where you might need post-processing to trim partial tokens.
[03:12] Mark: Latency — you mentioned p95 numbers in Console — what's typical for hosted?
[03:18] Jordan: For small prompts (under ~200 tokens) we often see p95 in the 100-250ms range on our hosted endpoints depending on model choice. Larger contexts increase latency. We'll share more precise benchmark data; Priya will run a Lakeside sample run.
[03:33] Aisha: And cost—how do we think about tokens vs calls vs batch?
[03:38] Priya: Tokens are the primary unit for generation cost. We also expose batching features in Redwood Optimize and autoscaling to amortize fixed overheads. For high QPS you can get better per-token economics with batching and prefix caching (KV cache).
[03:54] Tom: Is KV cache available on Hosted or only Dedicated?
[03:58] Priya: We have prefix and KV caching in Hosted for common sequences; Dedicated gives more control for larger caches and custom eviction policies. Apologies if I say "Redwood Dedicate" — transcript note — I meant Dedicated.
[04:10] Mark: Security and compliance — we need SOC2 and SSO with SAML. Also customer data residency is a question.
[04:16] Jordan: We have SOC2 Type II and SAML SSO, plus RBAC and audit logs in the Console. For data residency, our hosted regions cover NA and EU; we can discuss Private or Dedicated if you need on-prem or VPC-only access. We'll attach the security pack after the call.
[04:33] Aisha: Great. Any encryption/KMS support?
[04:36] Priya: We integrate with cloud KMS providers and customer-managed keys on Dedicated/Private deployments. Hosted has encryption at rest by default and managed KMS.
[04:45] Mark: Back to retries — what patterns do you recommend? Exponential backoff? Idempotency + at most 3 retries?
[04:52] Priya: Yes, exponential backoff with jitter and a max of 2-3 retries is typical. Use idempotency keys to avoid double-side effects. For streaming, it's trickier — sometimes re-requesting the tail is best. We can share sample retry pseudocode.
[05:06] Jordan: We also add client-side timeout guards to avoid waiting forever; server enforces a max runtime and returns an error code you can handle.
[05:13] Tom: Do you expose retryable vs non-retryable error codes in SDK?
[05:18] Priya: Yes, SDKs classify errors; transient 5xx are flagged retryable, rate-limit responses include a Retry-After header. We also provide tokenized usage metrics so you can see cost impact.
[05:31] Mark: We expected a POC — timeline wise we want to spin up a pilot in 2-4 weeks. What do you need from us?
[05:38] Jordan: Ideal: sample payloads, target SLAs (p95), expected QPS, and any security constraints. We'll run a benchmark, share pricing and propose a scoped POC.
[05:48] Aisha: We'll surface sample prompts and some real sessions.
[05:52] Tom: One more question — what about function calling / structured outputs for product info?
[05:58] Priya: We support structured output and function/tool calling patterns; stop sequences and response schemas help keep outputs clean. For high-precision answers, you can combine retrieval and generation; Redwood has reranking and embeddings features as well.
[06:14] Jordan: Quick demo wrap — here's a streaming example showing partial token deltas and how client renders as they arrive. Please note occasional spelling in transcript, like "K V cache" vs "KV cache".
[06:28] [demo finishes]
[06:33] Mark: Looks promising. A few concerns about predictable cost — can we cap monthly spend or set alerts?
[06:39] Jordan: Yes, Console supports quota limits, per-route budgets, and alerting. For larger commitments, Dedicated reserved capacity gives predictable unit pricing.
[06:49] Aisha: Any built-in tools to estimate monthly cost for our workload?
[06:53] Priya: We have a usage estimator and Redwood Optimize will suggest batching/quantization and model variants to reduce cost. We can run your sample to get a concrete estimate.
[07:04] Mark: Ok let's recap next steps.
[07:07] Jordan: Priya will run bench with your dataset and share p50/p95 latency and cost projection. I will send pricing and security docs today. We'll schedule POC kickoff for week of 3/23.
[07:18] Aisha: Sounds good.
[07:20] Tom: Thanks everyone.
[07:22] Jordan: Thanks, talk soon.

Transcript notes: occasional speaker mislabels and small transcription errors (proper nouns, acronyms). References to shared artifacts: "pricing deck" link placeholder, "security pack (SOC2)" link placeholder, "benchmark spreadsheet" (will be shared).
